title: Build AI Systems for Discernment, Not Approval - Angel Ortmann Lee, Duolingo

summary: Angel Ortmann Lee introduces human-in-the-loop AI as a framework where humans supervise or decide for automated systems to ensure accuracy, safety, and ethical outcomes. However, as AI integrates into daily life—GPS navigation, search summaries, coding suggestions—people increasingly trust AI outputs with diminishing scrutiny. A Wharton study identified cognitive surrender: humans forgo deliberation and adopt AI output with minimal scrutiny. 80% of participants accepted wrong AI answers; performance rose +25 points when AI was right but fell -15 when wrong. At the Duolingo English Test (DET)—a fully online, remotely proctored high-stakes exam trusted by 6,000 programs—the team studied this through their copy-typing cheating detection system. In a controlled experiment, they presented completely legitimate sessions to experienced proctors with fabricated AI cheating alerts. Despite proctors scoring above 90% on accuracy calibration, they accepted 50% of fake signals—a coin-flip rate indicating strong automation bias. The model had a 1% false positive rate; the problem was interaction design. A guideline copy change—framing AI signals as preliminary and requiring independent video evidence—produced a 21% increase in rejection rates, moving from 50% to 71% correctly identified as legitimate. The talk reframes the human-AI loop as cyclical: model output shapes interaction, which shapes behavior, which yields data feeding model improvement. A headphone-detection example illustrates how a single yes/no CTA conflates two questions: whether the model correctly detected headphones and whether a violation occurred. Breaking it into two questions yields better data—for instance, a hearing aid is a true signal but not a violation. A writing tutor example contrasts an overwhelming 400-line LLM response with a Duolingo-style inline markup using green, yellow, and red annotations tied to specific text, mimicking human feedback patterns. A coding agent example identifies two rubber-stamping patterns: giant diffs approved then debugged later, and excessive per-file approval pings. The ideal resembles a junior developer who plans, asks good questions, surfaces assumptions, and breaks work into reviewable PRs, capturing rich structured data about assumptions, tradeoffs, and preferences rather than binary accept/reject signals. The talk presents four design principles: (1) engineer the reasoning—reframe the human as investigator, surface assumptions, weigh trade-offs, build friction where stakes are high; (2) match friction to stakes—deliberate slowness for high-stakes decisions, frictionless for low-stakes chat; (3) treat every interaction as a label—capture the diff between accepted and modified output, monitor questions as trust signals; (4) define success metrics proactively rather than retrofitting evaluation. Implementation methods include structured inputs/outputs, highlighting assumptions, and building review gates. The talk closes by emphasizing that friction and review gates cause people to take ownership of decisions rather than treating AI as a supplanting force, and that collecting explicit, nuanced feedback at correct touch points—beyond simple thumbs up/down—directly drives model improvement. The core message: design for discernment, because the fix is engineering the interaction itself, not a better model or more oversight.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Human-in-the-Loop AI Definition
sections.summary: Angel introduces the talk title and defines human-in-the-loop AI as a framework where humans participate in operation, supervision, or decision-making for automated systems to ensure accuracy, safety, and ethical outcomes.

sections.title: Cognitive Surrender & Wharton Study
sections.summary: Discusses how AI integration into daily life increases trust and decreases caution. Introduces the Wharton study on cognitive surrender, where humans adopt AI output with minimal scrutiny. 80% accepted wrong AI answers; performance rose +25 points when AI was right but fell -15 when wrong.

sections.title: Duolingo English Test & Copy-Typing Experiment
sections.summary: Describes the DET as a high-stakes online English proficiency exam trusted by 6,000 programs, with AI-assisted monitoring and human proctor review. Details the copy-typing detection system and the controlled experiment injecting fabricated AI alerts into legitimate sessions.

sections.title: Results & Interaction Design Solution
sections.summary: Proctors accepted 50% of fake signals despite >90% accuracy calibration, indicating automation bias. The model had 1% false positive rate; proctors were skilled. A copy change reframing AI signals as preliminary and requiring independent evidence produced a 21% increase in rejection rates, from 50% to 71% correctly identified as legitimate.

sections.title: Implications: Cyclical Loop, Data Flywheel & Headphone Example
sections.summary: Frames human-AI interaction as cyclical: interactions yield data feeding model improvements. Intentional design creates a virtuous cycle of honest labels and better models; poor design creates a vicious cycle of rubber-stamping. Introduces a headphone-detection example showing how a single yes/no CTA conflates model accuracy with cheating determination.

sections.title: Headphone Example Resolution, Writing Tutor & Coding Agent Patterns
sections.summary: Completes the headphone example: breaking the yes/no into two questions separates model accuracy from violation status, using hearing aids as a case where detection is correct but no violation should be flagged. A writing tutor example contrasts a 400-line overwhelming LLM response with a Duolingo-style inline markup using green/yellow/red annotations tied to specific text, mimicking human academic feedback. A coding agent example identifies two rubber-stamping patterns—giant diffs approved then debugged later, and excessive per-file approval pings—and proposes an ideal agent that acts like a junior developer who plans, asks good questions, surfaces assumptions, and breaks PRs into reviewable pieces, capturing rich structured data rather than binary accept/reject signals.

sections.title: Design Principles: Engineer Reasoning, Match Friction, Interaction-as-Label, Define Success
sections.summary: Presents four design principles. (1) Engineer the reasoning: reframe humans as investigators not validators, surface assumptions early, weigh trade-offs explicitly, build friction for sustained attention where stakes are high. (2) Match friction to stakes: deliberate slowness with review gates for high-stakes decisions like DET; frictionless for low-stakes chat. (3) Every interaction is already a label: capture the diff between accepted and modified output to avoid false signals polluting datasets; monitor questions and follow-ups as trust indicators. (4) Stop asking how to evaluate the model—define success metrics proactively and design interactions to capture the needed evidence. Implementation methods include structured inputs/outputs (forms, tables, markup UIs), highlighting assumptions proactively, and building friction and review gates.

sections.title: Conclusion: Ownership, Nuanced Feedback & Design for Discernment
sections.summary: Closes by emphasizing that friction and review gates cause people to take ownership of decisions rather than treating AI as supplanting human judgment. Collecting explicit, nuanced feedback at correct touch points—beyond simple thumbs up/down—directly drives model improvement because every interaction feeds the next model generation. The core thesis: design for discernment, because the fix is engineering the interaction itself, not a better model or more oversight.
